title: The siege
hookLine: grievances grow, rebels surround his house, and he refuses to let blood be shed for him

cards: The street outside the caliph's house is full of armed men, and they are not foreign soldiers. They are Muslims, from Egypt and the garrison towns of Iraq, with complaints about governors, appointments and money.
They have camped in Medina, and they want Uthman to step down. He will not take off what God has put on him, he says. So they close in on his house.

Inside are a few companions and young men, among them, the histories say, Hasan, the Prophet's grandson, sent by Ali to guard the door. They have swords. And the old man inside tells them to put the swords away.

teach.b: Fitnah. In the Qur'an the word carries trial, temptation and testing, and the lexicons connect the root with smelting gold in fire to see what is real.
Later Muslims also use it for civil strife, Muslim against Muslim, a test of a different kind. The histories give the name to the years that begin at Uthman's door. Why did he refuse a defense?
The sources point back to the Prophet. Bukhari records a day when the Prophet sat at a well and the companions came one by one asking to enter. For Abu Bakr: give him the good news of paradise.
For Uthman: the good news of paradise, with a trial that will befall him. Uthman answered, the report says: God is the one whose help is sought.

teach.h: DO NOT TAKE OFF THE SHIRT.
teach.b: And Tirmidhi records the Prophet telling Uthman that God might clothe him in a shirt, and if people wanted him to take it off, he should not.
Uthman read these as a calling: keep the office, and don't let Muslims kill Muslims to save his life.

teach.h: GO HOME. LAY DOWN YOUR WEAPON.
teach.b: So, the histories report, he told those guarding him to go home, and told the servants who would fight that whoever laid down his weapon was free. Readers have argued ever since.
Holiness, or handing the city to the rebels? Sunni tradition honors it as the restraint of a martyr. Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances he had not answered.
The sources agree on the core: he forbade fighting for him.

how: The histories name the siege of Uthman as the start of the fitnah; Sunni teachers cite his refusal to let Muslims fight on his behalf, and Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances behind the revolt.

o: a formal charge brought against a ruler
a trial or test; later, strife among Muslims
a holy war fought to defend the caliph

s: the men at Uthman's door were a foreign army
they were Muslims from Egypt and Iraq with complaints about his rule.
Uthman told his defenders to go home
the histories report he forbade fighting for him and freed servants who laid down their weapons.
fitnah only ever means civil war
in the Qur'an it carries trial, temptation and testing; strife among Muslims is a later, narrower use.

games.q: you're Uthman. rebels surround your house. loyal men inside have swords drawn and ask for your word to fight. what do you say?
o: fight; the caliph must be defended.
put the swords away and go home.
games.why: the histories report he forbade them to fight, refusing to let Muslims kill Muslims to save his life, and refused to step down.

practice: Bring to mind one live conflict: a family thread, a neighbor, a coworker, a comment section. Find the move you've been tempted to make, the reply that would bring in your allies, and set it down, without giving up what's right.
If you pray, you can ask for help in the trial.

wordCard.voice: Fitnah. Trial and testing in the Qur'an, and later the name for strife among Muslims, beginning, the histories say, with the siege of Uthman's house. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: trial, testing; later, strife within the community.

carryVoice: Your line: he forbade fighting for him. Restraint can be its own kind of courage. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.
